claims.claim: American spelling and punctuation are house style, with Merriam-Webster's first-listed variant winning (toward, backward).
claims.source: D&D Style Guide: Writing and Editing, Version 1.08a (2018; 'updated January 2019')
D&D Style Guide: Writing and Editing, Version 1.08a (2018; 'updated January 2019')

claims.claim: Negative contractions (don't, can't, wasn't) are encouraged; other contractions are used with care where they could be misread.
claims.source: D&D Style Guide: Writing and Editing, Version 1.08a (2018; 'updated January 2019')
claims.quote: We encourage the use of contractions formed with “not,”

claims.claim: 'Non-' is hyphenated before fantasy races (non-elf, non-drow) but closed for 'nonhuman', and numeral-plus-abbreviation compounds are never hyphenated (100 gp treasure).
claims.source: D&D Style Guide: Writing and Editing, Version 1.08a (2018; 'updated January 2019')

claims.claim: Possessives follow Chicago 17th edition (7.16–29), including names ending in an unpronounced s.
claims.source: D&D Style Guide: Writing and Editing, Version 1.08a (2018; 'updated January 2019')
claims.quote: We follow the approach in the seventeenth edition

claims.feature: words used as words / foreign words
claims.claim: English words used as words go in quotation marks; a non-English word, real or invented, is italicized when used as a word.
claims.source: D&D Style Guide: Writing and Editing, Version 1.08a (2018; 'updated January 2019')
claims.quote: is italicized when used as a word

claims.claim: Vertical lists are introduced by a complete sentence ending in a colon, items start with a capital, and closing punctuation appears only if items are full sentences.
claims.source: D&D Style Guide: Writing and Editing, Version 1.08a (2018; 'updated January 2019')
claims.quote: introduce it with a complete sentence ending with a colon

claims.claim: Whole numbers zero through one hundred are spelled out in prose (Chicago 9.2), with the usual exceptions for units, parts of a book, dates, and times.
claims.source: D&D Style Guide: Writing and Editing, Version 1.08a (2018; 'updated January 2019')
claims.quote: we spell out whole numbers from zero to one hundred

claims.claim: 'Percent' is written as a word except in tables or tight lists; percentile dice are 'd100', never 'd%'.
claims.source: D&D Style Guide: Writing and Editing, Version 1.08a (2018; 'updated January 2019')
claims.quote: Use the word “percent,” rather than the symbol %

claims.claim: Cross-references are used judiciously; chapters are cited by number, subsections and sidebars by quoted title, tables by unquoted title.
claims.source: D&D Style Guide: Writing and Editing, Version 1.08a (2018; 'updated January 2019')

claims.claim: Appendices are lettered, not numbered, and cited like chapters ('see appendix A').
claims.source: D&D Style Guide: Writing and Editing, Version 1.08a (2018; 'updated January 2019')
claims.quote: We use letters, not numbers, for appendices

claims.claim: Page references are avoided because they are hand-added at galley and break across reprints; cross-product page references are especially discouraged.
claims.source: D&D Style Guide: Writing and Editing, Version 1.08a (2018; 'updated January 2019')
claims.quote: We avoid page references as much as possible

claims.claim: In D&D fiction, thoughts and psionic speech may be set in italics, quotes, or plain type at the author's discretion, a reversal of the older policy.
claims.source: D&D Style Guide: Writing and Editing, Version 1.08a (2018; 'updated January 2019')
claims.quote: Aesthetics and clarity should dictate appropriate usage

claims.claim: A character is 'on' a plane of existence but 'in' a plane named without the word 'plane' (in Elysium).
claims.source: D&D Style Guide: Writing and Editing, Version 1.08a (2018; 'updated January 2019')

claims.claim: Ability scores, action names, class features, feats, skills, languages, planes, and race/monster traits are capitalized as proper game terms.
claims.source: D&D Style Guide: Writing and Editing, Version 1.08a (2018; 'updated January 2019')

verdicts.note: Quote verbatim p.4 'Variant Spellings'. All limbs on page: 'We use American style for spelling and punctuation'; 'If a word has variants in Webster's, we use the one printed first (regardless of alphabetical order), except as noted in the D&D word list'; both examples toward/backward present. Merriam-Webster's Collegiate 11th named as a primary house resource on p.1.

Quote verbatim p.4 under heading 'The Serial Comma'. 'Require' = mandatory; the Mystra/Elminster example shows the ambiguity rationale. '(Oxford)' in the claim is only a synonym for 'serial comma', not a separate assertion the page must carry.

verdicts.trueWording: We encourage the use of contractions formed with “not,”
verdicts.note: Quote verbatim p.4. Page continues 'such as "don't," "can't," and "wasn't" (see Chicago 5.105). Use other contractions with care, especially any contraction that can be misread.' Both limbs — negatives encouraged, others used with care where misreadable — are explicit.

Quote verbatim p.4. Page: 'The prefix is hyphenated in front of many of our fantasy races: non-elf, non-dwarf, non-orc, non-drow (but nonhuman, as in Webster's).' Numeral limb also explicit: 'we don't hyphenate a compound composed of a numeral and an abbreviation. So, it's a "100 gp treasure," not a "100-gp treasure."' The page's hedge 'many of our fantasy races' is exactly the nonhuman exception the claim itself carries.

verdicts.trueWording: We follow the approach in the seventeenth edition
verdicts.note: Quote verbatim p.4 under 'Possessives', followed on-page by '(see Chicago 7.16–29)'. The unpronounced-s limb is explicit: 'particularly those that involve words that end with an unpronounced s, as in "Descartes."'

verdicts.trueWording: is italicized when used as a word
verdicts.note: Quote verbatim p.4. English limb explicit: 'Our style for words used as words is to enclose them in quotes if the words are English (see Chicago 7.63).' 'real or invented' matches 'A non-English word, whether from the real world or a D&D world, is italicized when used as a word.'

verdicts.trueWording: introduce it with a complete sentence ending with a colon
verdicts.note: Quote verbatim p.4. Page scopes it to 'a bulleted list—or any other vertical list, such as a numbered one', and adds 'We begin each list item with a capital letter. Use closing punctuation in an item only if the list is composed of complete sentences.' All three limbs present.

verdicts.trueWording: we spell out whole numbers from zero to one hundred
verdicts.note: Quote verbatim p.5, preceded by 'We follow the general rule for numerals that is presented in Chicago 9.2.' All four named exceptions appear in the page's bulleted exception list: units of measure {6'3", 5 gp, 3 lb.}, parts of a book {chapter 2, page 34, table 9}, dates, and times. 'In prose' is the page's own contrast: 'Numerals in Rules. In rules writing, we use numerals more often.'

verdicts.trueWording: Use the word “percent,” rather than the symbol %
verdicts.note: Quote verbatim p.5. Exception limb explicit: 'You can break this rule in a table, as well as in a list where space is tight.' Dice limb explicit: 'Also, the abbreviation we use for percentile dice is d100, not d%.'

Quote verbatim p.5 ('They are useful tools that can be easily overused'). Chapter limb p.5: 'When you refer to a chapter, use its number.' Subsection/sidebar and table limbs p.6: 'When you refer to a subsection, including a sidebar, use its title in quotes. A table title is not enclosed in quotes.'

verdicts.trueWording: We use letters, not numbers, for appendices
verdicts.note: Quote verbatim p.5. Cited-like-chapters limb explicit: 'References to appendices should follow the same principles that we follow for chapter references', with the on-page example '• See appendix A for definition of each condition.'

verdicts.trueWording: We avoid page references as much as possible
verdicts.note: Quote verbatim, though it sits on p.6 of the PDF, not the p.5 the claim record cites — a locator slip, not a substance error. Both reasons on page: '(they must be added by hand during galley review), and they invite error'; and 'Referencing a particular page in another product is especially ill-advised; that product's pagination could change in a reprint or a new edition.'

verdicts.trueWording: a change from our previous policy
verdicts.note: Quote 'Aesthetics and clarity should dictate appropriate usage' is verbatim on p.6, and the discretion limbs are fully supported: 'In D&D fiction, authors are free to use italics, quotation marks, or no distinguishing typography to present a character's thoughts or psionic communication (see Chicago 13.43).' But the page says only '(This is a change from our previous policy.)' — the word 'reversal' is absent, and the guide never states what the previous policy was, so the claim's characterization of the direction of the change is not established by the page.
verdicts.unsupportedLimb: 'a reversal of the older policy' — page says only 'a change from our previous policy' and never states the prior rule

verdicts.note: Quote verbatim p.6 under 'Planes of Existence'. Both limbs explicit: 'A character is on a plane of existence. For example, "He was trapped on the Plane of Fire." But a character is in a plane when it is referred to by name without the word "plane."'

verdicts.trueWording: Action names {the Attack action, the Dash action}
verdicts.note: Quote verbatim p.6 in the 'Terms to Capitalize' list. Every one of the eight categories the claim names is on that list: Ability scores {Strength, Intelligence}; Action names; Class features {Sneak Attack, Rage}; Feats {Loremaster}; Languages {Common, Dwarvish, Elvish}; Planes of existence {the Abyss, the Nine Hells}; Skills {Arcana, Perception}; Traits in races and monsters {Aquatic, Keen Senses}. Scoped on page to the RPG: 'In the RPG, certain terms receive special typographic treatment.'
